text: Every AWS account is born with one identity already in it: the root user, created the moment you sign up with an email address and a password. Root isn't an IAM user and it can't be deleted — it's the account itself, wearing a login screen, with complete, unrestricted access to everything inside it.

Root logs in with an email and password, not a username, and it comes with no permission boundary at all — it can touch every service, every resource, and every dollar on the bill, by design. There's no policy you can attach to limit it, the way you can with an IAM identity. That's exactly why AWS's own guidance says root should almost never be the identity you're signed in as while doing real work. One leaked password and an attacker owns the entire account, servers and billing alike.

The fix is a short sequence you run once, right after creating the account. Enable multi-factor authentication on root first, so a password alone isn't enough to sign in as it. Then create an IAM user with administrator permissions and start using that identity for everyday work instead. Finally, store the root password and MFA device somewhere safe — a password manager or a physical safe — and stop touching root for anything routine. From there on, root becomes something you reach for a few times a year, not something you log into every morning.

A handful of account-level actions genuinely can't be delegated and still require root: closing the AWS account entirely, changing root's own email or password, viewing certain billing and tax documents, changing the account's support plan, and restoring an IAM user's access if they've locked themselves out. Everything else — servers, storage, IAM policies, logs — belongs to the admin user you just created.

That's the root user: powerful by necessity, dangerous by default, and meant to be locked away rather than used. Next, Lesson 2 covers the identities you'll actually use day to day — IAM users, the groups that organize them, and the policies that spell out exactly what each one is allowed to do.
